segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set you free from the law of sin and death.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For what the law could not do, weak as it was through the flesh, God did: sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and as a sin offering, he condemned sin in the flesh,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who live according to the Spirit, on the things of the Spirit.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the mindset of the flesh is death, but the mindset of the Spirit is life and peace,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: because the mindset of the flesh is hostility toward God: it does not submit to God’s law, nor indeed can it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And those who are in the flesh cannot please God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. And if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, that person does not belong to him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if Christ is in you, then though the body is dead because of sin, the Spirit is life because of righteousness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies because of his Spirit who dwells in you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, brothers and sisters, we are debtors, but not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for if you live according to the flesh, you are going to die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For you did not receive a spirit of slavery, leading back into fear; rather, you received the Spirit of adoption, in whom we cry out, “Abba, Father!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Spirit himself testifies with our spirit that we are children of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And if children, then heirs too: heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ, if indeed we suffer with him so that we may also be glorified with him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I consider that the sufferings of the present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is going to be revealed to us.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the creation in eager expectation awaits the revealing of the sons of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the creation was subjected to futility, not willingly but because of the one who subjected it, in hope

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: that the creation itself will also be set free from its slavery to decay into the freedom of the glory of the children of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we know that the whole creation has been groaning together and suffering birth pains together until now.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And not only that, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, also groan within ourselves as we await adoption, the redemption of our bodies.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For in hope we were saved. But hope that is seen is not hope; for who hopes for what they see?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with endurance.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In the same way, the Spirit also helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes with wordless groans,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he who searches hearts knows what the mindset of the Spirit is, because he intercedes for the holy ones in accordance with God’s will.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For those he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he would be the firstborn among many brothers and sisters.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And those he predestined he also called; and those he called he also justified; and those he justified he also glorified.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who is against us?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also, with him, freely give us all things?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Who will bring a charge against God’s chosen ones? It is God who justifies.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Who is the one to condemn? It is Christ who died, or rather, who was raised, who is also at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Will affliction, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or sword?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As it is written,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “For your sake we are being put to death all day long; we were considered sheep for slaughter.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I am convinced that neither death nor life, neither angels nor rulers, neither things present nor things to come, nor powers,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: neither height nor depth, nor any other created thing, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.

notes.phrase: those who are in Christ Jesus
notes.traditional: who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit (added in the King James Version)
notes.note: Later manuscripts add “who do not walk according to the flesh but according to the Spirit” at the end of this verse. The earliest witnesses lack the words, and they are generally thought to have been copied in from verse 4.
The “you” is singular. Many manuscripts read “me”, which continues the first-person voice of chapter 7, and a few read “us”. The evidence is closely divided; the edition translated here reads “you”.

In Paul “flesh” often means more than the physical body. Here and through verse 13 it is human nature in its weakness and its bent away from God, treated almost as a power that people can live “in” or “according to”. The traditional word is kept because the contrast with “Spirit” depends on it.

The Greek is literally “concerning sin”. In the Greek Old Testament this phrase is the regular term for the sin offering, and many scholars think Paul's readers would have heard it that way. Others take it more generally, “to deal with sin”; the question remains disputed.

notes.traditional: righteous requirement; righteousness of the law
notes.note: Greek has a single word-family where English has two (righteous/just, righteousness/justice, justify). “Righteous requirement” here, “righteousness” in verse 10 and “justified” in verses 30 and 33 all translate related Greek words, a connection English cannot show.

notes.traditional: the Spirit is life; your spirit is alive
notes.note: The Greek word can be the human spirit or God's Spirit, and it is not marked either way. Some translations read “your spirit is alive”, in contrast with the body. Since Paul writes “is life”, not “is alive”, and the Spirit gives life in verses 2 and 11, many scholars take it as the Spirit of God, as here.

notes.phrase: because of his Spirit who dwells in you
notes.traditional: through his Spirit who dwells in you
notes.note: The manuscripts are divided between two forms that differ only in grammatical case. One means “because of his Spirit”, the reading of the edition translated here; the other means “through his Spirit”, which most English versions follow. Both are ancient and well attested, and either way the indwelling Spirit is the pledge of resurrection.

Paul's word is “sons”, which here includes women and men alike; in verses 16, 17 and 21 he switches to the neutral “children”. “Sons” is kept because it ties believers to “his own Son” (verses 3, 29, 32) and to “adoption” (verses 15, 23), a word built on “son” that denoted the legal adoption of an heir. Some modern versions use “children” throughout.

Abba is Aramaic for “father”, the address Jesus used in prayer (Mark 14:36). Paul keeps the Aramaic word and puts the Greek for “Father” beside it, which suggests the cry was known in that form even in Greek-speaking congregations.

Paul does not name who subjected creation. Most interpreters understand God, with reference to the curse on the ground in Genesis 3, since only God could subject it “in hope”. A minority think of Adam, whose disobedience brought the curse.

The traditional “saints” now suggests canonised individuals or people of unusual virtue. Paul uses the word for all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Greek Old Testament's language for Israel. Other translations use “God's people” or keep “saints”.

notes.phrase: all things work together for good
notes.traditional: all things work together for good
notes.note: The Greek can also be read with God as the unstated subject: “he works all things together for good” or “in all things he works for good”. Some early manuscripts add “God” to make that explicit. The rendering here takes “all things” as the subject, which is the simplest reading of the shorter text.

Ancient manuscripts had no punctuation, so the replies in verses 33 and 34 can be read as statements, as here, or as further rhetorical questions: “Will God, who justifies? Will Christ, who died?” The sense is much the same either way, since no accuser or judge is left to stand against those God has vindicated.

candidates.reason: Recurs throughout Paul with a range from the physical body to human nature opposed to God, and translations vary between “flesh”, “sinful nature” and “human nature”.
The plural addressed to mixed congregations occurs in nearly every letter and needs one policy on “brothers” versus “brothers and sisters”, including figurative uses such as verse 29.
The Semitic idiom of “walking” for conduct recurs across Paul and John, and translations split between “walk” and “live”, which here would collide with the verb “to live” in verses 12 and 13.
Common across the New Testament and rendered variously as tribulation, affliction, trouble, suffering or distress; a reader would be misled by seeing it vary.
The traditional “elect” is now a theological term or political word; the choice between “elect” and “chosen” should be made once for the Gospels, Paul, 1 Peter and Revelation.
